clue.text: Blast! All because of a pirate!

parts.note: to blast a plant is to scorch or wither it, which is to sear it
when something is all done or finished, it is over

explanation.surface: Someone curses loudly because a pirate has caused all their troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blast!' reads as an oath but is the verb meaning scorch; 'because of a' simply links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rover of the sea is an old literary name for a buccaneer who plunders ships.

clue.text: May be sore about short, weight slice given

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters surround the next piece
may be suggests the word sore could be rearranged into another form

parts.note: ct is the short form of carat, a unit of weight for gems

explanation.surface: Someone may be aggrieved about being given a slice that weighs short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May be' rearranges SORE into SEOR, which goes 'about' CT.
explanation.definitionFit: A sector is a wedge-shaped portion of a circle, like a cut piece of pie.

clue.text: A service with edge in the Netherlands

parts.note: RN, the Royal Navy, is one of the armed services
a hem is the folded edge of cloth

explanation.surface: A military unit fighting along a border in Holland.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Navy is the senior service in Britain; Arnhem was the scene of a famous wartime airborne battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnhem is a Dutch city on the Rhine, so it lies within that country.

clue.text: Exercises inside but in full view

indicators.note: inside means one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: but can mean only, as in 'there were but two'
PE, physical education, means school exercises

explanation.surface: Working out indoors, yet visible to all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' is the old sense of merely.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something openly means doing it publicly, with nothing hidden.

clue.text: Conclude cross is at risk

parts.note: to conclude is to bring to an end
cross means annoyed, as does angered

explanation.surface: Finishing a cross-shaped thing puts it in danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like a noun but is the adjective meaning annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: A species or person in danger of harm or extinction is threatened.

clue.text: The doctor's paper knife

explanation.surface: A medical man's choice of blade for opening letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lancet is a famous British medical journal, and a lancet is also a small double-edged surgical blade.

clue.text: Main race possibly in the USA

indicators.note: possibly says the words could form something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Perhaps the chief contest takes place across the Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: Something belonging to or found in the United States is described by its national adjective.

clue.text: Honour a simple man of the cloth

parts.note: CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order
plain means simple or unadorned

explanation.surface: Paying tribute to a humble priest.
explanation.walkthrough: CH is Companion of Honour, a British honour conferred by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman, attached to a college, regiment or hospital, is a cleric, often called a man of the cloth.

clue.text: Complaisant about party backing a hard worker

indicators.note: backing means the preceding pieces run in reverse

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a lot is a group or party of people
the ant is proverbially industrious

explanation.surface: An obliging person thinks well of a group supporting a diligent employee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns RE + LOT into TOLER, to which ANT is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Being accommodating and indulgent of others means putting up with them patiently.

clue.text: Does without nurse, but struggles

indicators.note: used in the old sense of outside, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: to do someone is to swindle them, so does means cons
to nurse a patient is to tend them

explanation.surface: A carer manages without a nurse but finds it hard going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like a plain verb but is the slang sense of cheat; 'without' means outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who contends strives or battles against an opponent or difficulty.

clue.text: Don't forget to pay another visit

explanation.surface: A reminder to remember to drop in on someone again.
explanation.definitionFit: To recall is to remember, and split as re-call it means to call on someone once more.

clue.text: Left the country, but not by sea

definitions.text: Left the country, but not by sea

parts.words: Left the country, but not by sea
parts.note: describes a departure across borders made on roads or rails rather than by ship

explanation.surface: An emigrant chose to travel abroad by land instead of sailing.
explanation.definitionFit: Travel done across terrain rather than over water is by the land route.

clue.text: Writer for whom work's just a grind?

definitions.text: for whom work's just a grind?

explanation.surface: An author complains that their job is nothing but drudgery.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur and Henry Miller were American authors, and a miller spends his working days grinding corn.

clue.text: Records the demolition of Dorset town

indicators.note: demolition breaks the words down so they can be rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: Documents showing a town in Dorset being knocked down.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorchester is the county town of Dorset, a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorchester is the county town of Dorset, Thomas Hardy's Casterbridge.

clue.text: Make over in a not over-way-out fashion

indicators.note: a way-out fashion is a wild, unconventional style, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Redecorating in a style that is not too outlandish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'way-out fashion' signals rearranging IN plus A NOT OVER; 'Make over' is read as a noun, a makeover.
explanation.definitionFit: A makeover of a house is a restoration and refurbishment to improve its condition.

clue.text: Case found by strike breaker without key

parts.note: a scab is a worker who refuses to join a strike
bar means except or without
D is a musical key

explanation.surface: A legal case brought by a strike breaker without a key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests a law suit but is a sheath; 'without' is BAR, as in 'bar none'.
explanation.definitionFit: A scabbard is the sheath that holds a sword's blade.

clue.text: They pry with some hesitation into golf, club's set-up

indicators.note: into means the hesitation goes inside the reversed club name
set up in a down clue means written upwards, so read backwards

parts.note: a spoon is an old golf club with a lofted face, and the plural gives spoons
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: Nosy people hesitantly look into how a golf club is organised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set-up' reverses SPOONS to SNOOPS, and ER goes 'into' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Busybodies who nose into others' affairs are prying people.

clue.text: Abuse-when for example a sum is incorrect

indicators.note: incorrect means the letters are set out wrongly, in a new order

parts.note: eg abbreviates exempli gratia, for example
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Misuse arises whenever a calculation goes wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Misusage is wrong or improper use, that is maltreatment.

clue.text: Private communication of faith

explanation.surface: A secret message about belief.
explanation.definitionFit: A confidence is a secret told privately, and confidence also means trust or belief in someone.

clue.text: Stop engineers going over-seas

indicators.note: in a down clue going over means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: RE are the Royal Engineers
the main is an old word for the open sea

explanation.surface: Military engineers heading overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop' means stay, as in 'stop the night'.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay put somewhere is to continue to be there.

clue.text: Minor showing discourtesy

explanation.surface: A youngster being rude.
explanation.definitionFit: Slight means small or trivial, and a slight is also a snub or insult.

clue.text: Remove from the shade — let everyone enjoy it

indicators.note: from tells us the answer is taken from within the following words

explanation.surface: Take it out of the shade so all can enjoy it in the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'shaDE LET Everyone'; 'enjoy it' only completes the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To delete is to erase or strike out text.

clue.text: Minor villain going on foot

parts.note: B denotes second rank, as in a B-movie or B-list, so something minor
a rogue is a dishonest rascal or villain

explanation.surface: A small-time crook walks off on foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going on foot' is the definition: a heavy shoe is what goes on your foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A brogue is a sturdy leather shoe with decorative perforations, worn on the foot.

clue.text: A rousing militaristic call

parts.note: a rousing call here is literally one that wakes soldiers, sounded on a bugle at dawn

explanation.surface: A stirring military summons.
explanation.definitionFit: Reveille is the morning bugle signal that wakes troops in camp.

clue.text: Rings right-minded painter on return

indicators.note: on return means the joined pieces are read backwards

parts.note: someone right-minded in the sense of sound in mind is sane
RA, Royal Academician, is a standard abbreviation for a painter

explanation.surface: A sensible artist going back to the boxing rings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on return' turns SANERA round to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Circus and boxing rings are enclosed spaces for performance or contest, like stadiums.

clue.text: Put the squeeze on alien holding British money

indicators.note: holding means one word encloses the other

parts.note: something alien is foreign or unfamiliar, that is strange
L stands for the pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Extorting cash from a foreigner who carries pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put the squeeze on' suggests extortion but means literally to throttle.
explanation.definitionFit: To throttle someone is to compress their neck, literally squeezing.

clue.text: Broke, so discouraged

explanation.surface: Having no money leaves someone disheartened.
explanation.definitionFit: Dashed means smashed to pieces, and hopes that are dashed leave a person dejected.

clue.text: Beast keeping catch dark

indicators.note: keeping means one word holds the other inside

parts.note: a brute is a savage animal or beast
to net a fish is to catch it

explanation.surface: An animal hangs on to its prey in the darkness.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman with dark brown hair is described this way.
